comments.text:
Very solid review, especially those cost/ frame graphs!

Too bad you didn't test the old RX 6800 (none XT, 16 GB) with Raytracing! It would have been very interesting, if the older card could also keep up with the 7700 XT with RT in like Spiderman!
For me, the secret winner here is the RX 6800, especially used. During Corona for many people it was no problem buying used. So I don't see any reason against it today either!

It pushes the same performance as the 7700 XT as it seems (only none RT data here in that video for comparison) and is a good deal cheaper at current street prices, but offers more VRAM! And when looking at "older" titles like The Last of Us Part 1 which already uses nearly 12 Gigs of VRAM 17:41 it should be more future proof to go with 16 Gigs!
Yes, the testing was in 4K ... but when looking at tech demos with UE5 the upcoming possibilities with higher textures and more details is a valid thing to come.

So for me: this kind of performance for a 1440p card is worth like 300 - 350 bucks. And above 300 bucks I wouldn't consider a GPU with less than 16 Gigs VRAM.
Just shy below 300 bucks a RX 6700 XT with 12 Gigs still is a fair option, though.

So if you take the average 1440p frame rate of all the cards represented here ( 12:16 ) , which is 99.17 fps, and use that to normalize the cost per frame (CPF * (99.17 / FPS)), the best bang for the buck is the 7900 XT (normalized = $3.95), followed by the 6950 XT (normalized = $4.13), followed by the 7800 XT (normalized = $4.25).

The 7700 XT (normalized = $5.39) is in the middle, and the 4060 Ti 16gb (normalized = $6.97) is the worst aside from the two 20-series cards (both over $14 normalized).

The 6700 XT (normalized = $5.98), which has the best cost per frame actually scores worse than the 7700 XT once normalized because while the cost per frame is low, the average frame is lower than everything except for the 20-series cards.

The problem with normalizing using this method is the fact that it's highly-dependent on the selection of cards used, especially if there are outliers at either end of the spectrum.  But I find it useful when determining relative value/longevity... like based on this, I wouldn't buy a 6700 XT even though it might represent the best performance value since it might not deliver acceptable performance across a wide range of games and it might not be future-proof.

Given the 10% reduction in cores, and a slight increase in frequency, I wouldn't have expected a 16% drop in performance from the 7800XT at 1440p. Is it possible it's being held back that much by memory bandwidth? We've seen that before from Nvidia's current GPU's. 

My thinking is that raw processing power should be ~10% less than the 7800XT, but with memory bandwidth decreased by 30% and Infinity Cache bandwidth decreased by 26%, it looks like an issue of not having enough bandwidth to feed data to the cores. Perhaps AMD could have used the same 19.5Gbps memory from the 7800XT on the 7700XT. VRAM is exceedingly cheap, and that would have increased memory bandwidth by ~8%. This would mean that instead of the 7700XT having 30% less memory bandwidth than the 7800XT, it would only be 25% less, aka equal to the decrease in bus size (256bit vs 192bit). 

I wonder if overclocking the VRAM would lead to a larger increase in performance relative to an equal % overclock to the GPU's core frequency.

comments.text:
I think you may be completely right, but the 7700 XT should probably still be ignored by consumers at 450 USD unless they're really desperate for a GPU and/or Starfield, and for some reason can't find anything better in their region. 

I'm fairly certain that AMD can make a higher profit selling us the 7800 XT at 500 than they can by selling us the 7700 XT at 400, and even at 400, the 7700 XT probably STILL wouldn't be a better value to most users than the 7800 XT is at 500, especially within the context of the cost of an entire new system. Cutting down flawless Navi 32 compute chiplets to make more 7700 XTs would also just be a waste, and they're already doing it to some extent, so I think it's arguably a good thing if AMD doesn't price the 7700 XT too low, because it will actually help to push people to buy what is ultimately the better value product. 

That being said, AMD left a significant gap between the lowly 7600 and the 7800 XT, leaving no true successor for the 6600 and 6600 XT, and certainly COULD have made an additional GPU and graphics card to slot in between them, probably with 12GB of Vram. They could have used a monolithic 6nm or 5nm design, but I'm guessing the R and D cost of yet another chiplet design would have been hard for them to justify. 

A 5nm monolithic design with 12GB of Vram might have cost just as much in R and D costs, or even more (as far as I know), but would have had by far the best power efficiency of any discrete RDNA3 card, would have made for an excellent laptop card, and also would have been a great niche product for small form-factor builds. Maybe their excess stock of RDNA2 GPUs is what led them to not bother with such a product, but it's hard not to think that it would have been good even if it was only used for laptops. If any large laptop maker had lobbied for such a product to be made, and committed to buying a large order of them, AMD probably happily would have done it, and then some of them likely would have found their way into higher clocked desktop versions at some point.

Yeah, the 6950 XT launched at an outrageously high price, and we only got a good price on it later on because AMD had a ton of leftover stock and needed to price it competitively against the RTX 4000 series. It's definitely still a competitive value at 600 or less, but I think the 7800 XT is a better value at 500, in part because of better power consumption, but also because of architectural improvements which will probably improve even more over the next year or two (hopefully including better quality upscaling at some point). 

It's not unusual for previous gen cards to get heavily discounted before a lot of the next generation cards even get released. 

If you want to actually assess how much the current gen improves value over the previous gen, it doesn't make sense to compare to heavily discounted pricing of the previous generation, and makes far more sense to compare pricing to launch MSRP pricing of previous gen cards.

The 7800 XT offers a significant improvement in value over the 6000 series cards, just not their heavily discounted prices which you can currently find today in the US. HOWEVER, the 6000 series isn't nearly as widely available at great prices in a lot of places outside of the US. 

The 6800 XT launched at 650 in 2020, which is equivalent to about 770 USD today, which is about what the 7900 XT currently goes for, which makes sense, as that's the true successor to the 6800 XT. 

The 6700 XT launched at 480 USD in early 2021, which is equivalent to 540 USD today, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster, with 33% more Vram. Even if we assume that the 6700 XT was originally planned to launch closer to about 430 or even 400, 400 USD in early 2021 is equivalent to about 450 USD today, so the 7800 XT is still offering a fairly significant improvement in value even over that hypothetical launch price.

They recommend a 700W psu for a 7800xt as it depends on your whole setup and not all power supplies are created equal.  It's best to have at least the recommended just in case the gpu or the system sees a quick spike in power draw as it can cause the system to shut down / restart.  Some power supplies are more sensitive to quick massive spikes than others too and the protection built into them can be tripped sometimes.  Does this mean you can get by with a 650w high quality, probably and you can always limit the gpu or undervolt things if needed temporary until you get a bigger psu.  I would always recommend getting more than enough PSU though so you have upgrade-ability in the the future.  If you get a 1000w psu, it doesn't mean it will pull or use 1000w.  The system will only draw what it needs.

AMD's marketing team knew exactly what they were doing: Take the flack over the price, but have a chance of selling out 6800XTs and 6800s without dumping them (much) further in price. Even if you assume that the 6700 XT was probably originally planned to launch closer to around 430 or even 400, until the GPU shortage happened, 400 USD in early 2021 is equivalent to about 450 USD today, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster, has 33% more Vram, and various other features and improvements, including what appears to be better quality coolers than most models of the 6700 XT, so the 7800 XT still offers a significant improvement in value even over that hypothetical price. 

The 5700 XT, released four years ago for 400 USD, is equivalent to about 480 USD today, and the reference model had a lame blower cooler, but that was still considered a great value at the time (especially non-blower style coolers for the same or slightly higher price). The 7800 XT is around 90% faster, with double the Vram and massively improved power efficiency, so we're definitely still seeing significant improvement in value over time, but it's also definitely true that the rate of improvement is slowing down, and that's largely because of Moore's law no longer holding true with manufacturing costs relative to performance increases. 

It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, but AMD is certainly not primarily responsible for that, though we can give them at least some portion of the blame for that. AMD is also offering us worse value products in the lower-mid-range than before, unless you count the heavily discounted 6700 XT, but that isn't even available at good prices in a lot of regions, and will likely mostly sell out in less than a year from now. Nvidia is also offering worse value for everything below the 4070.
